# Perdition Gulch

## I.

The earth remembers what the people prefer to forget, and this particular earth—the cracked alluvial plate beneath Perdition Gulch, Nevada Territory—has been remembering for sixty million years, give or take an ice age. It remembers being seabed. It remembers the weight of a Cretaceous ocean pressing down like the hand of a god with nothing better to do. Now it is desert, which is only a sea that has forgotten its water, and the town atop it is a small and temporary assertion of human will against a landscape that has outlasted every prior assertion for epochs.

From a sufficient height—the height, say, of vultures, who have grown numerous this year—Perdition Gulch looks like a splinter driven into the hide of an animal too large to notice. Fourteen buildings. A main street that is not a street so much as a consensus, a mutual agreement among structures to face the same direction. South of town, the mine tailings rise in pale heaps like a new and lesser mountain range assembled by committee. North, the well. The well is the reason for everything. Without the well there is no Perdition Gulch, and this year the well has begun to form its own opinion about the arrangement.

Six inches. The water dropped six inches in August, and it is now September, and it has dropped again—another four since the last measuring—and Nestor Grieve, who owns the dry-goods store and is by default the town's record-keeper of secular matters, has taken to measuring it every morning with a knotted rope and a face that suggests he is receiving news of a relative's prolonged illness. The dust has opinions too. It coats the windows in a film so fine and persistent that Ada Polk, who runs the boarding house, has stopped wiping them clean. It grits between teeth. It works into the stitching of boots and the mechanisms of watches and the corners of eyes.

All of this is ordinary. Drought is ordinary. Dust is ordinary. What is not ordinary—what has never been ordinary, though the town has arranged itself around the fact so thoroughly that the arrangement has taken on the appearance of normalcy—is the council.

They are five. They do not call themselves a council. Nobody elected them. They are simply the people to whom other people bring problems that have no ordinary solutions, and this has been true since 1879, when the five of them were fewer, and then more, and then five, and then settled.

The healer is Mattias Kern. He is forty-six this year, though the body he wears could belong to a man of thirty. He has dark, square hands, eyes the color of creek mud, and the posture of a man who has never had reason to flinch. He is mending a fence rail behind the smithy when the nail goes in. A common nail, slightly rusted, driven upward through a split plank by the pressure of his palm. It enters the meat at the base of his left thumb—a puncture one-quarter inch across, less wound than insult.

He pulls his hand back. Looks at it.

He has been shot twice in the abdomen and once in the throat. He walked into a mine shaft during the collapse of '82 and pulled two men out through a gap that should have killed all three of them. The throat shot is an interesting story: the bullet passed through his larynx and out the back of his neck, and Maya Abano, who saw it happen, remembers a sound like a man coughing underwater, and then Mattias standing, the hole already closing, the blood running upward as if confused about the direction of gravity, re-entering the wound as the flesh sealed over it like clay pressed smooth by a thumb.

Now a nail has entered his hand and the blood is running in the correct and irreversible direction, which is down, toward the earth, and the earth is drinking it the way it drinks everything this year—instantly and completely—and the wound is looking up at him with the stupid, inert openness of an ordinary hole in ordinary skin.

He waits. He has never had to wait for this. The waiting itself is new, as unfamiliar as the pain, which is so mundane that he has no framework for interpreting it—a dull, honest throb, the body's tedious complaint.

He waits eight seconds. Twenty. A minute. The blood slows, because blood does slow eventually, even ordinary blood, through no magic but the simple chemistry of coagulation—platelets arriving at the site like bureaucrats to a crisis, slow and insufficient but eventually adequate.

The flesh does not close.

He goes inside the smithy, where no one is working because it is midday and hot. He opens a pine cabinet and finds a rag that smells of turpentine and iron, and he wraps his hand, and he wraps it carefully, not because the wound requires care but because the wrapping is a practice of concealment and concealment requires precision. He ties the rag with a knot a sailor would recognize.

He tells no one.

This is the first silence, though it will not be the last, and the narrator—patient as the rock, old as the sea that preceded the rock—has seen this particular species of silence before, in this particular town, and knows what it produces.

---

## II.

Begin earlier. Begin in 1879, before the town had a name that anyone used with a straight face, when the gulch was just a mining camp called Sulfur Flat and the buildings were canvas over timber and the well was new.

Maya Abano arrived first. Or rather, Maya Abano was already there, which is a different thing than arriving. She worked in the assay office, recording weights and grades in a hand so precise it looked typeset, and she remembered everything—not in the way that diligent people remember, not by effort or repetition, but in the way that a daguerreotype remembers: completely, instantly, and without her consent. The label on a tin of peaches glimpsed through a window as she passed at age seven. The exact number of boards in the floor of her mother's house in Santa Fe (one hundred and forty-three, with a knot in the sixty-ninth that resembled a closed eye). The particular gray of the sky over Perdition Gulch at 6:47 on the morning of March 3, 1874, distinguishable in her mind from the gray at 6:47 on March 4, which had more yellow in it, a sulfurous tinge, though no one else alive could have identified the difference.

She did not know what she was. She knew only that she could not stop seeing, could not stop keeping, and that the accumulation of perfect images had made her precise in conversation and impossible in intimacy. To know someone the way Maya knew everyone—to recall every contradiction, every small cruelty, every promise broken and reconstructed and broken again—is to be incapable of the strategic forgetting on which all human relationships depend.

She saw Mattias Kern take a bullet in October.

This requires specificity: it was the fourteenth of October, a Wednesday, and the light was the amber of late afternoon, and the man who shot Mattias was named Polk—no relation to Ada, who would arrive two years later—and his given name was Clement, and he was drunk on a corn whiskey that smelled of lye and poor decisions, and Mattias was simply standing in the path of the bullet, which had been intended for a dog that had bitten Clement Polk's son. The bullet struck Mattias in the left side, between the eighth and ninth ribs. Maya was forty feet away. She saw him fold at the waist as anyone would and then she saw him straighten as no one should, and she saw the blood—red darker than arterial, almost black in the amber light—appear on his shirt in a bloom the shape of a child's hand and then stop, not slow but stop, as if a faucet had been turned, and the shirt remained stained but the body beneath it was whole and Mattias was looking at the stain with an expression she had seen only on the faces of people caught in a lie.

He looked up and found her watching.

She did not look away. The not-looking-away was the first thing that passed between them. In a town where everyone had the decency to unsee what should not be seen—a survival skill in mining camps, where men disappeared into shafts and debts and each other's grudges—Maya Abano stood forty feet away and saw all of it and did not pretend otherwise.

Three days later she said to him, in the assay office, with the door closed: "You should have died."

"I know," he said.

"You didn't."

"I know."

"How."

It was not a question. It was an offering—an opening in which he could, if he chose, say the true thing that would make them complicit. He could also lie, which would make them strangers forever.

He said, "I don't know how. I know that it's always been this way."

And Maya said, "I remember everything. Every single thing." The sentence left her mouth with the velocity of something held too long—not a confession but an exhalation, the releasing of a breath she had drawn at age seven when the 143 boards and the knothole entered her mind and would not leave.

They stared at each other in the assay office. Outside, someone was hammering. The light through the single window made a trapezoid on the floor that Maya would remember—the exact angle, the dust motes, the way the shadow of the window frame fell across Mattias's left boot—for the rest of her natural life, and then somewhat beyond it, until the remembering itself began to fail, but that is later, that is now, and we are still in then.

---

The child arrived in December. He was eight years old. His name was Toby, though he had not been Toby before and would not feel like a Toby later; it was a name given to him by the woman who brought him to Sulfur Flat, a woman named Frances Dunlap who said she was his aunt and who thought, all the time, in a loud and disorganized slurry that Toby could not stop hearing, that the child was not right, that the child was perhaps dangerous, that she wished her sister had not died and left her with this creature who looked at you as if he could see behind your teeth.

He could not see behind anyone's teeth. He could hear behind them, which was worse.

The world, for Toby, was layered. There was the surface—the sounds that came from mouths, shaped into words with whatever imprecision mouths allow—and then beneath it, constant as water beneath ice, the other sounds: the actual thoughts, the unedited interiors, the raw noise of consciousness before it has been dressed for company. In a room with one other person, this was manageable. In a room with ten it was a roar. In a room with fifty—a dining hall, a Sunday service, a town meeting—it was a cacophony so dense that individual thoughts blurred into a composite hum, a single chord of collective interiority, and the chord was almost always scored in the key of fear.

He met Maya and Mattias because Frances Dunlap brought him to the assay office to ask about work, and while Frances was talking to the clerk about wages, Toby turned to Maya and said: "You don't have to be scared of the numbers. They stay because you make them stay. You're the one doing it."

Maya, who had never told anyone about the numbers—the running tally, the involuntary census of every detail—looked down at this child. He was undersized and sharp-boned and had the eyes of something feral that had learned to sit still.

"I can hear you thinking about it," the boy said. "Right now. You're counting the buttons on my coat."

She was. There were nine. One was wood and the rest were bone and the wood one was third from the top and it was newer than the others, a replacement.

"Eight," the child said, answering the thought she had not spoken. "There were eight before. She sewed on the wood one in Reno."

Frances Dunlap came back from the clerk's window and took Toby's arm and said they were leaving, and Toby went, and Maya stood in the assay office with her perfect memory of nine buttons and a child who had read her mind with the casualness of reading a signpost, and she went to Mattias that evening and said, "There's another one."

---

The twins arrived in spring. They came out of the desert from the east, which was the wrong direction—the direction from which no one came because there was nothing to come from, only salt flats and heat and the mathematical certainty of death by exposure. They walked into Sulfur Flat on a Tuesday afternoon, a man and a woman, both in their late twenties, both dark-haired, both sun-ruined to the same degree, wearing clothes that had been good a hundred miles ago and were now garments in theory only. They carried one canteen between them. They were not speaking.

They did not need to speak. This was the thing that was immediately visible to anyone who watched them closely, and Toby, sitting on the step of the boarding house with his too-old eyes, watched them very closely. They moved in a coordination so fluid that it passed beyond the merely fraternal and into something structural: when one turned left, the other compensated right, not in response but simultaneously, the way the two hands of a single body reach for the same object without negotiating.

The man's name was Abel. The woman's name was Nell. They introduced themselves to Nestor Grieve at the dry-goods store and asked about lodging, and Nestor thought—loudly, in the way that incurious men think, with the thoughts sitting on the surface like oil on water—that they were man and wife, and Toby, across the street, heard this and also heard what Abel and Nell were actually thinking, which was:

*Tell him,* Abel thought, and the thought had no direction; it was not aimed at Nell because it did not need to be aimed; it was simply present in both their minds at once, the way a sound is present in both ears—

*Not yet,* and this was Nell, or this was Abel thinking in Nell's register, or this was the place between them where their thinking overlapped and became indistinguishable, and the child Toby heard it as one voice in two bodies and he sat on the step and gripped his knees and thought: *Oh.*

---

The back room of the dry-goods store smelled of lye and grain dust and mice. There was one window, painted shut in a year no one could recall, and the paint had yellowed and cracked in a pattern that Maya could describe down to the individual fissure but that everyone else perceived as merely old. Five grain sacks sat against the east wall. A table, unvarnished pine, scarred with the half-moons of cup bottoms and the straight lines of blade marks. Four chairs. Mattias stood. He always stood.

They came to the room separately, at intervals, in the way people come to places they are not sure they should be. Maya first—she had arranged it. Then Mattias, who entered and positioned himself against the wall nearest the door, which was the habit of a man who had learned that exits matter even when you cannot be killed. Then Toby, brought by Maya, the child walking with the stiff dignity of someone who understands that his presence is conditional on adult permission. Then the twins together, because the twins did everything together, and they sat in two of the four chairs and folded their hands in the same gesture at the same moment and looked at the others with the same waiting expression.

"I asked everyone to come," Maya said, "because I believe we are—"

"The same kind of thing," Nell said.

"—something," Maya finished, and the word she'd planned to use—*similar*—had been rendered inadequate by Nell's more precise offering.

What followed was not a conversation so much as a series of doors opening in a hallway where every door had been locked since childhood. Mattias described the bullet. He described other bullets, and a knife, and a fall from a rail trestle that should have broken his spine. He described the feeling—the moment of damage followed by a warmth that moved beneath the skin like a hand under a sheet, pressing everything back into place. He described the loneliness of it, though he did not use that word. He said: "You stop telling people after the second time. The first time, they think they saw wrong. The second time, they think you're the devil."
